blocks.html: as broader distribution of psychology concepts continues in mainstream media, one line of reasoning that bothers me the most is the idea of detaching yourself from the outcome being the end all be all.

i find myself agreeing and digressing from this line of thinking- a lot of it is just a matter of convenience of the issue to me on a personal level. sometimes we have problems we’re happy to think a long time about (yc or a16z?!) but at the same time many problems are equally unpleasant to delve into (does this girl want me back? will i ever be happy? etc.) some problems, i am more than happy to play out the different outcomes in my head and think hard about its impact, but an equal number, if not more, i cannot stand to think of. i think this is true across most people.
detaching yourself from the outcome, in my eyes does/is for any of the following:
a) a coping mechanism because you cannot stand to think of the infinite possibilities of how a situation can play out.
b) you truly don’t gaf (very rare)
mainstream media juxtaposes the idea of detaching yourself from the outcome (a stoic connotated concept on instagram) with manifestation (an often metaphysical connotated concept).

i often find myself struggling with this idea of ‘manifestation’ as opposed to detachment. many argue that you must consistently imagine yourself in the position you wanna be in, with the wins you wanna have, with the successes you want to have- only then can it come true. the notion that the universe listens to you, and gives you what you ask for.

this is quite interesting to me. raised as a practicing hindu, even still, i believe in the concept of karma- you get what you deserve. how you treat others is how you get treated. put out good, good you will receive. therefore it is technically hard for me to deny the validity of an argument that the universe listens to your ‘manifestations’.

internally, i find them two concepts extraordinarily hard to reconcile within myself. on whether manifestation is real/has any effect, i don’t know. a lot of times i look back at significant events in my life, and interestingly enough, many of my ‘wins’ are things i dwelled on and told myself would happen- even if it was in an unserious capacity. but my heart and my brain has a hard time reconciling this concept of manifestation with whatever i was doing could be described as.

i think they are all just problems of scale and value, it’s just hard to be exact. in my opinion, the bigger an issue is, the bigger a question is, the closer it is to emotional aspects of my life, i wish not to dwell on it. i believe in detaching from the outcome.

from the objective however (i.e, i WILL exit with $1b+, i WILL win conrad etc.), i think a certain amount of wishful thinking is beneficial. i struggle with calling this manifestation because that’s simply not how i would describe it. to me, it’s just thinking something through. just thought, imagination, day dreaming.
on day dreaming however, i think there is much value to letting your imagination roam free.

on detaching yourself from the outcome i am quite undecided. i do not know how to address such a principle as across different stages, events, even hours of my life i find myself digressing from both detachment and the vice versa.

one of my favorite movies growing up was heat, starring de niro and al pacino. i remember watching it the first time hearing de niro’s Neil McCauley say “don’t let yourself get attached to anything you are not willing to walk out on in 30 seconds flat if you feel the heat around the corner”.

the idea of him fading his old life so quickly was bizarre to me, but the underlying concept of maintaining a permanent level of detachment from everything is quite interesting. my interpretation of this actually almost ignores the concept of detaching from the outcome, but is actually on a different principle: is it viable to maintain a consistent level of detachment from everything? is that the only way to be happy?

if you’re always detached to some nth degree in every relationship, you could argue you will never be fulfilled by a relationship, but the counterargument writes itself- you can never truly be hurt either. it could be called schrodinger’s happiness!

im not sure if it’s healthy and years after watching Heat, it’s hard to not think about it now given my (short)lived experiences. i think it’s a thesis centered around finding success in your own life as opposed to thoughts on relationships and happiness.

when de Niro’s character meets Pacino’s LAPD detective in the movie, they both realize that this philosophy is born entirely out of their quest for excellence, from their obsession with what they do. they’re so obsessed with their work, they’re so obsessed with the OUTCOME that they maintain a constant level of detachment from everything else. is it implying that to succeed you need to be detached?

ultimately it wouldn’t be crazy to say it works out for de Niro. he falls in love, yes, leaves her when the ‘heat’ comes around the corner, yes, but lives to build a new life another day. quid pro quo.

i don’t think it’s a bad principle for finding success in your life- specifically regarding the level of detachment you need to have. but the human part of me struggles with this. i think it’s so incredibly human to want, to care, to yearn, to love. to never experience that to the fullest degree, to have that be the price for ‘success’ is a dilemma that i don’t think i’ve decided on.

attachment, is destructive. de Niro experienced this exactly in the movie. he talks about how ‘you belong to me, and my survival depends on keeping you’. this forces the other to essentially live life on his terms. while not something most people will experience, i think every relationship has some sort of this tug and pull to have the other live life on SOME of their terms. we call this compromise. but the alternative is living a relationship devoid of this kind of attachment. hypothetically it means you are emotionally invulnerable- literally nothing can get to you. it’s also technically true freedom, you live life on your own terms because neither is holding the other hostage. this argument centers on the idea that objectively, all attachment is toxic.

i do think it is possible to have meaningful relationships in life and still succeed, but i think the argument to be made is that the most meaningful relationships are the ones that are the most detached (yet the most connected). almost paradoxically, what my point is that sometimes the strongest connection can exist because of total detachment. i still don’t know if i entirely believe that, however.
on whether to dwell or to detach on any major question in your life- i am undecided.
